panel: notebook: Under the hood > What g++ does with a returned local address; Lab step 2
what: The notebook says g++ 13's AddressSanitizer has stack-use-after-return switched off unless ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1 is set, but on this toolchain it is on by default.
evidence: Page: "in g++ 13 that check is off unless you run the program with ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1". Scratch test (/tmp/claude-0/-home-claude/7f030446-3270-51d4-abc1-d3638614f9af/scratchpad/review-content-cpp-13-15/t/uar.cpp: a global int* set to the address of a local in make(), then dereferenced in main), built with g++ 13.3 -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all and run under env -i with no ASAN_OPTIONS: "ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-use-after-return on address 0x7ffff4700020". With ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=0 the same binary prints a garbage number (1431673792) and exits 0. cpp/ch24.html footer also says its stack-use-after-return reports appeared without the option. This is new evidence for INTEGRATION_TODO 'From cpp ch24 (Remotes and Packed Lunches)' CONTRADICTION item; the TODO entry under 'From cpp ch13' (a .asanopts sidecar to capture the case) rests on the same wrong premise.
fix: Replace the sentence with: "AddressSanitizer also catches a note that outlives its function in general (stack-use-after-return); in g++ 13 here that check is on by default, and ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=0 switches it off." Better: capture a small program like uar.cpp (an out-parameter or global keeps the address so g++ doesn't null it) as a .san program and show its real report. In Lab step 2, change the ASAN_OPTIONS hint to say some compilers leave it off by default (as cpp ch24/ch25 do). Drop the .asanopts TODO item.

fix: Disclose it where readers run things: in the footer ("UBSan reports were captured with UBSAN_OPTIONS=print_stacktrace=1, which adds the #0/#1 lines") and in Lab step 2 ("run UBSAN_OPTIONS=print_stacktrace=1 ./after_move to see the call trail"). Cleanest: show it in the displayed run command via a .cmd step for UBSan programs. This is book-wide (every C++ chapter with a UBSan report), so one capture/engine-level decision plus a footer line per chapter.

what: States as fact that <memory> brings <utility> along. That's a libstdc++ detail, not a guarantee, and it teaches relying on a transitive include.
evidence: Page: "std::move(ada) (from <utility>, which <memory> brings along)". move_card.cpp includes <iostream>, <memory> and <string>, not <utility>. ch5's plan scope makes the opposite point (include what you use; transitive includes are not portable).
fix: "std::move comes from <utility>. Here <memory> happens to pull it in on this library, but include <utility> yourself", and add #include <utility> to the move programs (then recapture).

what: The explanation gets the order of a unique_ptr move-assignment backwards: the standard has a take the new pointer first and then delete the old box, not the other way round. Boss 1's hint already uses the correct order.
evidence: ex-owner explain: "a already holds a box (the 2), so that box is returned first (deleted), then a takes b's 1". [unique.ptr.single.modifiers] reset(p): "Assigns p to the stored pointer, and then, with the old value of the stored pointer, old_p, evaluates if (old_p) get_deleter()(old_p)" (move-assignment calls reset(u.release())). Not visible in this program's output (int has no destructor print).
fix: "a takes b's 1, and the box it was holding (the 2) is returned straight away".
